note.question: Should a firm target existing or rival customers with product-quality disclosure when it can also use purchase histories for personalized pricing?
note.overview: Two competing firms dynamically choose prices and costly disclosure thresholds while anticipating how first-period customer acquisition changes second-period poaching and retention. The paper solves the firms' rational-expectations equilibrium and an endogenous disclosure-format game that can be a prisoner's dilemma.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In period one the firms simultaneously set uniform prices and consumers choose a brand, generating observed customer segments. In period two the firms first simultaneously select uniform or segment-specific quality-disclosure thresholds, then set oldand new-customer prices, after which consumers observe available disclosures and prices, update quality beliefs, and stay with the prior firm or switch. Period-one customer acquisition changes the size of the profitable old-customer disclosure segment in period two. Disclosure to old customers is more valuable because they pay higher retention prices, whereas firms discount to poach rivals' customers.

components.label: Symmetric two-period rational-expectations equilibrium solved by backward induction
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Symmetric two-period rational-expectations equilibrium solved by backward induction. The paper derives period-two pricing best responses conditional on disclosure, solves equilibrium disclosure cutoffs using consumers' Bayesian beliefs, and then solves first-period prices while verifying no profitable deviation to asymmetric market shares. Proposition 4 adds the firms' endogenous choice between uniform and behavior-based disclosure.
